newsitem.title: GERMANY: Coalition seeks compromise in German tax talks.
newsitem.headline: Coalition seeks compromise in German tax talks.

text.p: Germany's ruling coalition said on Saturday it was open to compromise with the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) in key tax talks, but was also ready to walk out unless the SPD gave ground.

Chancellor Helmut Kohl's lieutenant Wolfgang Schaeuble told the newsweekly Der Spiegel that conditions for Tuesday's talks set out by SPD chairman Oskar Lafontaine suggested the opposition was not serious about reaching an agreement.

"We are ready to talk about all points, about all proposals," he said in an interview released ahead of publication on Monday, but "doubts remain whether the SPD is serious and wants to cooperate on a reform."
Kohl is due to meet Lafontaine on Tuesday in an attempt to restart talks that collapsed in February in a row over coal subsidies.
The government, which has pinned its hopes of fighting unemployment and reviving the economy on a massive tax overhaul, has accused the SPD of blocking reforms to damage its standing with voters.

Wolfgang Gerhardt, chairman of Kohl's junior coalition partners, the Free Democrats, said prospects had dimmed in the view of Lafontaine's demand for cuts in occupational insurance charges and an increase in child benefit.
"I would say the chances of an agreement are not all that high," Gerhardt said in an interview for Sunday's Bild am Sonntag newspaper.
"If no signals come on Tuesday that the SPD is ready to tie up a reform packet with us, further talks are a waste of time."
Chancellery Minister Friedrich Bohl told the Express newspaper he would break off the talks if the SPD offered no concrete proposals.

Lafontaine has set out five demands for his session with Kohl, including clarification of how much tax reforms will cost, a lower entry-level tax rate than the government has proposed and maintenance of a number of tax-free allowances.
Schaeuble, the parliamentary leader of Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), did not rule out compromise on these items.

He reiterated the coalition's willingness to offset cuts in social insurance or entry tax rate with increases in value added or fuel oil taxes but added that "the tax reform must in sum lead to a reduction."
Gerhardt criticised the call for higher child subsidies as "insincere and careless," saying higher payments to parents would have no impact on hiring and business investment.
The negotiations are intended to avoid a drawn-out battle in parliament, where the SPD can block tax measures through its upper house majority.
